section.title: The Presentation and the Boy Jesus
section.sectionRationale: Luke rounds off the infancy narrative with two temple scenes. First the infant Jesus is brought to Jerusalem to be presented to the Lord, where the aged Simeon takes Him up and sings that his eyes have seen God's salvation, a light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel, and where the prophetess Anna gives thanks. Then, twelve years later, the boy Jesus is found in the temple among the teachers, and speaks His first recorded words: I had to be in My Father's house. It is one movement about the child growing under the Law yet already marked as the Lord's own Son.
section.thesis: The child brought in poverty to the temple is God's own salvation, a light for the nations and glory for Israel, appointed for the fall and rising of many, so that even as He grows in obedience and wisdom, He is already about His Father's business.
section.frameNote: Seven beats: Jesus presented at the temple; Simeon's song of salvation; Simeon's prophecy to Mary; the thanksgiving of Anna; the return to Nazareth; the boy Jesus in His Father's house; and His growth in favor with God and man.

units.label: Jesus presented at the temple
units.note: according to the Law of Moses

verses.text: And when the time of purification according to the Law of Moses was complete, His parents brought Him to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord
(as it is written in the Law of the Lord: “Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord”),
and to offer the sacrifice specified in the Law of the Lord: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”

units.label: Simeon's song of salvation
units.note: my eyes have seen Your salvation

verses.text: Now there was a man in Jerusalem named Simeon, who was righteous and devout. He was waiting for the {{paraklesis|consolation}} of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him.
The Holy Spirit had revealed to him that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.
Led by the Spirit, he went into the temple courts. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for Him what was customary under the Law,
Simeon took Him in his arms and blessed God, saying:
“{{despotes|Sovereign Lord}}, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace.
For my eyes have seen Your {{soterion|salvation}},
which You have prepared in the sight of all people,
a {{phos|light}} for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel.”

units.label: Simeon's prophecy to Mary
units.note: a sword will pierce your soul

verses.text: The Child’s father and mother were amazed at what was spoken about Him.
Then Simeon blessed them and said to His mother Mary: “Behold, this Child is appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be spoken against,
so that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed, and a sword will pierce your soul as well.”
There was also a prophetess named Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, who was well along in years. She had been married for seven years,
and then was a widow to the age of eighty-four. She never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying.
Coming forward at that moment, she gave thanks to God and spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.

units.label: The return to Nazareth
units.note: the grace of God was upon Him

verses.text: When Jesus’ parents had done everything required by the Law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth.
And the Child grew and became strong. He was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon Him.

units.label: The boy Jesus in His Father's house
units.note: did you not know that I had to be in My Father's house

verses.text: Every year His parents went to Jerusalem for the Feast of the Passover.
And when He was twelve years old, they went up according to the custom of the Feast.
When those days were over and they were returning home, the boy Jesus remained behind in Jerusalem, but His parents were unaware He had stayed.
Assuming He was in their company, they traveled on for a day before they began to look for Him among their relatives and friends.
When they could not find Him, they returned to Jerusalem to search for Him.
Finally, after three days they found Him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.
And all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers.
When His parents saw Him, they were astonished. “Child, why have You done this to us?” His mother asked. “Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You.”
“Why were you looking for Me?” He asked. “Did you not know that I had to be in My Father’s house?”
But they did not understand the statement He was making to them.

units.label: Growing in favor with God and man

verses.text: Then He went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them. But His mother treasured up all these things in her heart.
And Jesus grew in {{sophia|wisdom}} and stature, and in favor with God and man.

paraklesis.gloss: Consolation, comfort, encouragement. Simeon was waiting for the consolation of Israel, a way of naming the messianic hope drawn from Isaiah's Comfort, comfort my people. The comfort God's people longed for arrives in the child Simeon holds.

despotes.gloss: Sovereign master, the owner with full authority over a household or servant, from which the English despot comes. Simeon addresses God as the Master who has complete right over his life, ready now to release His servant in peace.

soterion.gloss: Salvation, the saving act or the means of salvation. Simeon says his eyes have seen God's salvation, and he is looking at a baby. Salvation has a face and a name, prepared in the sight of all peoples.

phos.gloss: Light. The child is a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory to Israel, echoing Isaiah's servant given as a light to the nations. Luke's Gospel widens from Israel to all peoples, and here that reach is already announced.

sophia.gloss: Wisdom. Jesus grew in wisdom and stature and in favor with God and man. Truly human, He develops and matures, yet already at twelve His understanding astounds the teachers, for the wisdom of God is at home in Him.

basic.context: Obeying the Law of Moses, Joseph and Mary bring the infant Jesus to the temple to present Him to the Lord and offer the sacrifice of the poor, a pair of birds. There the devout old Simeon, promised he would see the Messiah, takes the child in his arms and sings that his eyes have seen God's salvation, a light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel. He warns Mary that this child will divide many and that a sword will pierce her own soul. The aged prophetess Anna gives thanks and speaks of Him to all awaiting redemption. Years later, at twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple, and when His anxious parents find Him, He asks why they searched, since He had to be in His Father's house. He returns to Nazareth, obedient and growing in wisdom.
basic.hermeneutics: Luke shows Jesus fully under the Law, brought up in a devout, poor family, yet already recognized by Spirit-led witnesses as God's salvation for the world. The two temple scenes bracket His childhood: at both, the temple is His Father's house, and both point beyond Israel to all peoples. The key questions are who this child is, why His coming brings both rising and falling and a piercing sword, and what His first words reveal about His identity.
basic.originalLanguages: Simeon waits for the paraklesis, the consolation, of Israel, and addresses God as despotes, Sovereign Master. His eyes have seen God's soterion, His salvation, a phos, a light, for the Gentiles and glory for Israel. Years later the boy Jesus grows in sophia, wisdom, and in favor with God and man.
basic.typology: The offering of the poor and the presentation of the firstborn place Jesus under the Law He came to fulfill. Simeon's song draws directly on Isaiah's servant, the light to the nations. The temple, called His Father's house, and the redemption of Jerusalem point to the greater redemption He will accomplish.
basic.christ: Simeon names the baby as God's own prepared salvation and the light of the world. At twelve, Jesus calls the temple His Father's house, the first hint in Luke of His unique divine sonship. He is the fulfillment both witnesses had waited for.
basic.god: God keeps His promise to Simeon and honors the patient devotion of Anna. He prepares His salvation in the sight of all peoples, reaching Gentile and Jew alike. He is faithful to the humble who wait for Him.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 42 and 49 give the servant as a light to the nations. Leviticus 12 sets out the purification offering. Malachi 3 speaks of the Lord suddenly coming to His temple. And John 2 shows Jesus again zealous for His Father's house.
basic.oneStory: The infancy narrative closes with salvation held in an old man's arms. The child under the Law is the light for the nations and the glory of Israel, destined to divide and to be pierced. Even as a boy He is about His Father's business, and the whole story now waits for Him to grow up and go to Jerusalem.

context.literary:
Luke 2:22-52 is a pair of temple scenes joined by two refrains of growth, verses 40 and 52. The first scene, verses 22 to 38, is a scene of recognition: two elderly people see the infant and speak. The second, verses 41 to 51, is a scene of misrecognition: the parents search anxiously for a child they thought they knew and then fail to understand what He tells them. Between and after them Luke inserts the summary of verse 40, 'the Child grew and became strong,' and the summary of verse 52, 'Jesus grew in wisdom and stature.' The two summaries enclose the second scene as a frame, and they also gather the whole infancy narrative into a calm close.

The passage is full of a care for the law of the Lord. Luke says it in verses 22, 23, 24, 27 and 39, five times in eighteen verses. Everything is done 'according to the Law.' That repetition has a purpose. Luke wants the reader to be sure that this family kept the commands, so that when Simeon sings of a light to the Gentiles, the child in his arms is unmistakably a faithful Israelite, a boy with a purification, a presentation and a pilgrimage behind him.

The Spirit's work is also emphasized, in a chain that places the Spirit three times on one man within three verses, 25 to 27: the Spirit was upon Simeon, the Spirit had revealed to him, and he was led by the Spirit into the temple. Simeon then speaks two oracles, a song to God in verses 29 to 32 and a prophecy to Mary in verses 34 and 35, and the difference is deliberate. The first looks outward in praise, the second looks inward at the cost.

The boy Jesus scene has two question-and-answer pairs, one between the teachers and Jesus, and one between Mary and Jesus. Mary says 'your father,' and Jesus says 'My Father.' The shift from 'your father' to 'My Father' is the hinge of the entire passage. And at the end, the one who has just claimed a higher Father returns to Nazareth and is obedient to the earthly ones, verse 51.
context.historical:
Leviticus 12 required a woman who had borne a son to wait forty days, seven of uncleanness and thirty-three of purification, and then to bring a lamb for a burnt offering and a bird for a sin offering, or, if she could not afford a lamb, two turtledoves or two young pigeons, Leviticus 12:2 to 8. Luke records that Mary offered the pair of birds, verse 24, which tells us the family's means. The presentation of the firstborn was a separate observance: every firstborn male belonged to the Lord, Exodus 13:2, and was to be redeemed, Exodus 13:13, with a price of five shekels, Numbers 18:15 and 16. Luke mentions the consecration but not the price, and many see in the account a conscious resemblance to Hannah's dedication of her son to the Lord's house at Shiloh, 1 Samuel 1:24 to 28.

Simeon and Anna belong to a stream of faithful waiting in Israel. Many in Jerusalem were looking for comfort and redemption, which is what Luke means by 'the consolation of Israel' and 'the redemption of Jerusalem,' verses 25 and 38. The long Roman occupation and the rule of the Herodian dynasty had turned that hope into something concrete. Anna is from the tribe of Asher, one of the northern tribes whose people had mostly disappeared from the record after the Assyrian conquest, though 2 Chronicles 30:11 shows some of Asher coming to Jerusalem to worship. Luke is telling us that the faithful remnant included descendants of tribes thought lost.

The boy Jesus story depends on the practice of the pilgrim feasts. The law asked the men of Israel to appear before the Lord three times a year, Deuteronomy 16:16, and Passover drew families from Galilee to Jerusalem in groups of relatives and neighbors. In such a caravan a twelve-year-old could easily be assumed to be traveling with other kin, as Luke says in verse 44, and the parents had gone a day's journey before they noticed. The temple courts were also a place of teaching, and it was ordinary for teachers to sit while students and visitors listened and asked questions. What was unusual was the quality of the questions and answers, which astonished the listeners, verse 47.
context.canonical:
The two scenes draw on several strands of Scripture. The presentation looks back to the law of the firstborn, Exodus 13, and to the story of Samuel, whom Hannah brought to the sanctuary. Luke's growth summaries use the very wording applied to Samuel in 1 Samuel 2:26, 'the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man,' which Luke 2:52 closely echoes. Where Samuel was a child dedicated to the temple who would anoint a king, Jesus is a child who is the King.

Simeon's song uses Isaiah. 'A light for revelation to the Gentiles' recalls the Servant who is a light to the nations, Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6, and the phrase 'in the sight of all peoples' recalls Isaiah 52:10, where all the ends of the earth see the salvation of God. His prophecy to Mary takes a different line, the stone of stumbling of Isaiah 8:14 and 15, which the apostles apply to Christ, Romans 9:32 and 33 and 1 Peter 2:6 to 8. Malachi's prophecy that the Lord will suddenly come to His temple, Malachi 3:1, also hangs over the scene, since the Lord comes to the temple in the arms of a poor couple.

The boy Jesus' first words are taken up in the later Gospel. At the Passover He cleansed the temple and called it 'My Father's house,' John 2:16, and in Luke 19:46 He says 'My house will be a house of prayer.' The language of divine necessity in 'I had to' is repeated at Luke 4:43, 9:22, 13:33 and 24:44 to 47, where the Scriptures themselves require that the Christ suffer and rise. Anna's 'redemption of Jerusalem' is picked up by the disciples on the Emmaus road who had hoped Jesus would redeem Israel, Luke 24:21, and the child who was found after three days in Jerusalem at Passover anticipates the Son who is raised on the third day.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke has two goals in this passage, and they pull in opposite directions in a way that he intends. The first is to show that Jesus is wholly Israelite. He is circumcised and named, presented and purified, taken to the feasts, and brought up in obedience. A reader who might think that a Gentile mission requires leaving the law behind is shown that the Savior of the nations arrived under the law, as Paul also says in Galatians 4:4.

The second goal is to show that this ordinary Israelite child is God's own salvation. Simeon names Him as such in his song, Anna talks of Him to everyone who is waiting for redemption, and the boy Himself speaks of God as His Father. Luke holds these two portraits side by side, the obedient child and the unique Son. He is not asking readers to choose between them. The boy who says 'I had to be in My Father's house' is the same who then goes down with His parents and is obedient to them.

Luke also means to warn. Simeon tells Mary that the child will cause division and be spoken against, and that a sword will pierce her too. Even before the first public word, Luke has made clear that this Gospel will not be received by everyone, and that following Him will cost even those closest to Him. Those who read the Gospel to find comfort are given the real picture from the start. The comfort Simeon waited for comes, but through a sign that will be opposed.

Finally, the passage ends with Mary treasuring all these things. Luke the researcher is signalling a source and a model: the memory of these events is being carried by someone who thought deeply about them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records what Joseph and Mary did under the law and what Jesus said at twelve. It does not tell parents to bring their children to the temple for a ceremony, and the Christian church has not read it that way, since the temple and its offerings have been fulfilled in Christ. What it does is demonstrate a pattern of life: this family did what the Lord commanded, and they did it at some cost, offering the sacrifice of the poor.

Simeon's prophecy is likewise a description of what would happen, not a prescription. A sword piercing Mary's soul is not a rule of motherhood, and the Gospels never present suffering as something to be chosen for its own sake. It is the reality that comes when a person stands close to the Son of God in a world that opposes Him, and Luke describes it so that no one will be surprised.

The boy Jesus' staying behind is not a model of childhood disobedience. Luke says plainly that the very next thing He did was go down to Nazareth and be obedient, verse 51. The point of the story is not that a young person should put religious interests above family but that this particular Son had a relationship with God that was unlike any other, and that even that did not make Him disregard His parents. The verbs 'grew' and 'was obedient' offer a quieter application: maturity in wisdom and favor develops in ordinary, submitted years.

debates.question: What is the sword that will pierce Mary's soul?

views.label: Her grief at the cross
views.case: Most readers take it as the pain Mary will feel when her Son is rejected and killed. It follows closely after the prophecy that He will be spoken against, and John 19:25 places Mary at the foot of the cross.

views.label: The divisive judgment of the child
views.case: The sentence in verse 35 links the sword with the revealing of the thoughts of many hearts. On this reading the sword is the cutting effect of Jesus on everyone, including Mary, who will at times be tested in her understanding, as when Jesus says that His true family are those who hear God's word and do it, Luke 8:19 to 21, and when He answers a blessing on His mother by blessing those who hear and obey, Luke 11:27 and 28.

views.label: Doubt or confusion at His passion
views.case: Some early readers took the sword to mean that even Mary would wrestle with doubt when her Son died. This is an old reading, but the text of Luke does not describe such a moment, so it goes beyond what is written.

debates.bearing: The first two views are not exclusive, and together they fit the sentence best. The phrase 'as well' tells us that Mary is placed within the circle of those who are tested by Him. Luke gives no hint of failure on her part, and he sees her again among the believers in Acts 1:14, so the sword is suffering and not unbelief.

debates.question: What does Jesus mean by 'in My Father's house' or 'about My Father's business'?

views.label: In My Father's house
views.case: The Greek says literally 'in the things of My Father,' and the context is the temple, where His parents have been searching. The translation 'house' is the most natural fit for the place where they found Him, and the BSB reads it so.

views.label: About My Father's affairs
views.case: The footnote allows 'about My Father's business.' The Greek phrase is a neuter plural with no noun, so it can mean the things that belong to the Father, and so His concerns and His work. This sense would reflect the later pattern in the Gospels, where Jesus describes His work as doing the Father's will, John 4:34.

debates.bearing: The ambiguity may be deliberate. The place and the mission cannot be separated, since the temple is where the Father's work is most visibly centered. In either case the contrast between 'your father' of Mary's reproach and 'My Father' in the answer is the point, as it is the first indication in Luke that Jesus knows God as His Father in a way no one else does.

debates.question: What is meant by 'the rise and fall of many in Israel'?

views.label: Some fall and others rise
views.case: On this reading the child divides Israel into two groups: those who stumble over Him, as in Isaiah 8:14 and 15, and those who are lifted up by Him. This fits the later experience of the Gospels and the application of Isaiah's stone to Christ in Romans 9:32 and 33.

views.label: The same people fall and then rise
views.case: Others note that the Greek has a single preposition governing both nouns, so that 'fall and rising' may describe one movement, a humbling that leads to restoration, as Jesus later teaches that those who humble themselves will be exalted, Luke 14:11 and 18:14.

debates.bearing: Luke's Gospel shows both patterns. Some, like the Pharisees and scribes, stumble over Jesus, and others, like the tax collector and the repentant criminal, are raised. The second reading adds that even those who stumble can be restored, which is the hope of the cross.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke describes Simeon as dikaios and eulabes, 'righteous and devout,' in verse 25. The first word speaks of right standing before God and with others, and the second, eulabes, speaks of reverent, careful piety, a person who handles holy things with care. The pairing describes a man who is both upright and attentive. The wording 'was waiting for' translates a participle that suggests an ongoing expectation, the stance of someone who has been watching for years.

In verse 29 Simeon says, 'You now dismiss Your servant in peace,' using the verb apolyo, which means to release or set free. It was used for the discharge of a slave or the relief of a sentry from his post, and it fits an old man who has been given an assignment to watch and who may now stand down. He is the doulos, the bond servant, speaking to the one who has the right to release him. The present tense gives the sense that the release is happening as he speaks, 'You are releasing.' The clause 'as You have promised' is literally 'according to Your word,' kata to rhema sou, the same phrase Mary used of her own obedience, Luke 1:38.

Verse 32 calls the child 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles,' using apokalypsis, from which comes our word 'apocalypse,' an unveiling. The light is not simply illumination but a drawing back of the curtain on the nations who had been kept in the dark. The 'glory' that follows is for Israel, so the two halves of the phrase stand side by side without competing.

In verse 34 the child 'is appointed,' using keitai, which is literally 'lies' or 'is set,' the way a stone is laid or a foundation is placed. The word for 'fall,' ptosis, and the word for 'rising,' anastasis, which Luke uses elsewhere of resurrection, are governed by a single preposition. The child is also 'a sign that will be spoken against,' semeion antilegomenon, from the verb antilego, 'to speak against.' It is the verb used in Acts 28:22 of the way the early church is everywhere spoken against, and the pattern of opposition begins with the Child.

The sword of verse 35 is rhomphaia, a large broad sword and not the short blade named by the common word machaira. It is the word used in Revelation 1:16 of the sword coming from the mouth of the risen Christ, and it speaks of something large and decisive. The 'thoughts' that are revealed are dialogismoi, the inward reasonings that Luke later shows Jesus perceiving, Luke 5:22 and 9:47.

In verse 49 Jesus says 'I had to,' using dei, 'it is necessary,' the word Luke uses throughout his Gospel for the divine necessity that governs the life of Jesus, as in Luke 9:22 and 24:26. His first recorded words already contain it. The final phrase of the sentence is en tois tou patros mou, 'in the things of My Father,' a construction with no noun, which is why translators divide between house and business.

Verse 51 says Jesus was 'obedient,' translating a present participle of hypotasso, 'being subject,' which suggests a continuing habit, and verse 52 says He 'grew,' using prokopto, a verb of advance, in the imperfect, so that He kept on progressing. The word translated 'stature' is helikia, which can also mean 'age,' so the phrase can be read as growing in wisdom and years.

typology.type: The firstborn presented at the sanctuary
typology.fulfillment: Every firstborn male in Israel belonged to the Lord because of the night when the firstborn of Egypt died and Israel's were spared, Exodus 13:11 to 15, and Hannah brought Samuel to the Lord's house and left him there, 1 Samuel 1:24 to 28. Jesus is presented as the child who is truly the Lord's. The correspondence is that the child was given back to God, and the escalation is that this Firstborn was given not for a lifetime of temple service but for the redemption of others, 'to redeem those under the law,' Galatians 4:5. The type falls short in that the other firstborn were redeemed by five shekels, while this One redeems at the price of His own life, Mark 10:45.

Isaiah said the Lord of hosts would be a sanctuary to some and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to both houses of Israel, Isaiah 8:14 and 15. Simeon's saying that the child will cause the fall and rising of many draws on that picture. Paul says Israel stumbled over the stumbling stone, Romans 9:32 and 33, and Peter calls Christ the precious cornerstone to those who believe, and a stone of stumbling to those who do not, 1 Peter 2:6 to 8. The correspondence is complete, and the same person is both refuge and offense. The limit of the image is that a stone is passive, whereas the child will actively seek and call, Luke 19:10.

The Servant of the LORD in Isaiah is appointed as a light for the nations to open blind eyes, Isaiah 42:6 and 7, and the LORD says it is too small a thing for Him only to restore Israel, for He will make Him a light to bring salvation to the ends of the earth, Isaiah 49:6. Simeon sees the whole prophecy in a baby. Paul and Barnabas apply the same text to their own mission, Acts 13:47, because they are carrying out what the Servant began. The type finds its fullness in Jesus' claim, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, and falls short only in that the Servant in Isaiah suffers before the nations see, which Luke's passage already hints through the sword.

typology.type: The temple and the Lord who comes to it
typology.fulfillment: Malachi said the Lord whom the people sought would suddenly come to His temple, Malachi 3:1, and Haggai promised that the glory of the latter house would be greater than the former, Haggai 2:7 to 9. In Luke the Lord does come to the temple, as an infant carried by poor parents and as a boy who calls it His Father's house. The temple is the place of God's presence and its meeting with His people, and Jesus is that presence in person. He later speaks of His own body as the temple, John 2:19 to 21. The type falls short in that the building would be destroyed, while the true temple is raised on the third day.

study.christ:
Simeon's words are the first full statement in Luke about what Jesus is, and they are spoken by a man holding a baby. He calls Him 'Your salvation,' not 'a salvation from You' but God's own saving act, prepared in the sight of all peoples. Salvation in the Old Testament is something God does and something God is, as when Moses sings of Him, 'He has become my salvation,' Exodus 15:2. To say that a child is that salvation is to say that He shares in what only God does.

The passage then reveals His mission in two directions. To the nations He is a light that unveils what was hidden, and to Israel He is glory, the very thing that Israel's temple and history had been reaching toward. Neither is at the other's expense. Paul puts the double aim in terms of the Gentiles glorifying God for His mercy while Christ becomes a servant to the circumcised to confirm the promises, Romans 15:8 and 9. The child in Simeon's arms is the meeting of the two.

The passage reveals the cost. He is a sign that will be spoken against, a stone that makes some fall. If Luke 2:14 spoke of peace on earth, verse 34 says peace comes through conflict, because truth exposes hearts. The thoughts that are revealed are the thoughts about Him, and the cross will be the place where those thoughts are laid bare, as the passage in Isaiah says of the Servant, who is despised and rejected, Isaiah 53:3. Simeon's pause to speak to Mary of the sword is a sign that the road to the nations runs through suffering.

In the second scene the boy's words show His identity. 'My Father' is a striking and personal way of speaking of God. It shows a consciousness of sonship that the Gospel of John will explore at length. At the temple He says the Father's things are what He must be about, and at the end of the Gospel He will say that the Christ must suffer and enter His glory, Luke 24:26. The same necessity governs the child and the man.

The passage shows a Savior who is also truly human. He grows. He asks questions. He is subject to His parents. Hebrews says that although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered, Hebrews 5:8, and Luke's Gospel shows the long years before that, in which He grew in wisdom. The full humanity of Jesus is not a decoration on His deity but the way the salvation is accomplished.

A caution is in order. The apocryphal gospels fill these hidden years with miracles and stories, but Luke says only that He grew, was obedient and was favored by God and men. The restraint is itself a lesson: the Savior's hidden years were years of ordinary faithfulness, and they were sufficient.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who keeps a private promise. The Spirit had told Simeon that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ, and the old man is led into the temple at exactly the moment the parents bring in the child. God's timing is exact, and it reaches down to one aging person in a large city. The same attention is given to Anna, a widow of eighty-four who has spent her years in prayer and fasting. God is not too great to notice the faithful over many years of what looks like unanswered waiting.

It shows a God who is Sovereign Master, as Simeon names Him, and also the One who gives His servant peace. The title says He has absolute authority, and the context says He uses it to release His servant from watching. Sovereignty and tenderness are the same attribute at work. Simeon dismisses himself into the keeping of someone who is entirely trustworthy.

It shows a God who prepares salvation in public. He has made it ready 'in the sight of all peoples,' not as a secret for a few, and the child is destined to be a light to the Gentiles and glory to Israel. The doctrine of God that emerges is that He is the God of all the nations from the beginning, who chose Israel in order to bless the world, Genesis 12:3. This is as much a statement about God as about the Gentiles.

It shows a God who is realistic about a fallen world. He does not promise that His salvation will be welcomed by all. He appoints the child to cause rising and falling, and the spoken-against sign. Divine love does not mean that every response will be positive, and the Lord knows ahead of time what the cost will be. He does not hide it from Mary.

It shows a God who is Father in a unique sense. The boy says 'My Father,' and the Gospel will continue to present God as Father of the Son before He is Father of anyone else. The believer's own sonship is received through the Son, as Galatians 4:4 to 6 says, so the intimate language of the Father in the Gospel starts here.

It shows a God who honors small means. The family offers two birds, the offering of the poor, and the Lord accepts it, since it is according to the law He gave. The Spirit rests on an old worshiper and a widow in the courts, and the child grows in the ordinary way in a Galilean village.

For worship, Simeon's song has served the church as an evening prayer for centuries. It teaches believers to look at the end of the day, and even the end of life, with a peaceful conscience, since the One who promised has kept His word. A worshiper who has seen God's salvation can let go.

crossReferences.note: The law of purification after childbirth, with its provision that the woman who cannot afford a lamb may bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons. Luke 2:24 quotes the poorer offering, so the passage tells us that the Savior's family was poor and that they observed the law down to its provisions for the poor.

The firstborn of every womb belongs to the LORD and is redeemed, as a memorial of the night when the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt. Luke's mention of the Lord's law that every firstborn male shall be consecrated points to this redemption story. The Firstborn who is brought to the temple is Himself the One through whom a greater exodus is accomplished.

Hannah brings Samuel to the house of the LORD and says that she has dedicated him to the LORD for as long as he lives. Luke's presentation scene and his repeated growth summaries clearly echo Samuel, and the contrast is that Jesus is not dedicated to Eli's sanctuary but is Himself the Lord of the sanctuary.

The LORD appoints His Servant as a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind and to bring prisoners out of the dungeon. Simeon's phrase 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles' draws on this and sets a sleeping baby as the fulfillment of the Servant's task.

It is not enough for the Servant to restore the tribes of Jacob; the LORD will make Him a light for the nations to bring His salvation to the ends of the earth. Simeon's twofold description, revelation for Gentiles and glory for Israel, is a short version of this verse. Paul quotes it in Acts 13:47.

The LORD will be a sanctuary but also a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to both houses of Israel, and many will stumble and fall. Simeon's word that the child is set for the fall and rising of many draws on this stone. The apostles use the same text in Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8 for the response to Christ.

The Lord whom the people seek will suddenly come to His temple as the messenger of the covenant, and no one will stand easily on the day of His coming. In the temple scene the Lord comes quietly and the waiting remnant recognizes Him. The refining that Malachi describes begins with the child who exposes hearts.

The LORD promises to shake the nations and fill the house with glory so that the latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, and that He will provide peace in this place. Luke places the true glory of the temple in a child in Mary's arms, and Simeon's 'glory to Your people Israel' is its fulfillment.

Jesus drives out the sellers in the temple courts and calls the building 'My Father's house.' The language of Luke 2:49 returns in an adult setting, and the disciples recall that zeal for the Lord's house would consume Him. What the boy said quietly the man says with a whip of cords.

When Christ came into the world He said that a body had been prepared for Him and, 'I have come to do Your will, O God.' The boy's 'I had to' is an early statement of the same obedient purpose. Hebrews explains that the will He came to do was to offer Himself once for all.

The disciples on the road to Emmaus say that they had hoped Jesus would be the One to redeem Israel, and the risen Jesus tells them that the Christ had to suffer and enter His glory. Anna's 'redemption of Jerusalem' and the divine necessity of Luke 2:49 come to full explanation in this walk through the Scriptures.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible is a story of a people called to be a light to the world and a God who keeps coming to dwell with them. Eden was the first temple, and after the fall the cherubim stood at its gate. The tabernacle and the temple were the return of God's presence in a guarded form, and the prophets looked for the day when the Lord would come to His temple in glory and when the nations would stream to it. Luke 2:22 to 52 is a double visit to that temple in which the long-awaited arrival takes place quietly.

The passage answers the question of whether the promises to Abraham, David and the prophets had been abandoned. The temple is still standing, but the glory that once filled it has been absent for centuries, and Israel is under foreign rule. Simeon and Anna answer that God has been faithful all along. They hold in their arms and in their eyes what the people had been waiting for. The consolation of Israel and the redemption of Jerusalem are present, though not in the form anyone expected.

It also sets up the rest of the Gospel. The sword Simeon mentions will go through Mary at the cross. The sign that is spoken against will be spoken against by the leaders in the same city. The boy who knew that He must be in His Father's house will return as a man to that house, to teach and to be rejected. The Passover in which He is found foretells the Passover in which He gives His life. And the mission to the Gentiles, first described by Simeon, will be given to the church in Acts, Acts 13:47 and 26:23.

In the whole of the story, the passage is a moment where creation's design and the fall's damage meet a person in whom the design is restored. Adam was a son of God who failed, Luke 3:38, and Israel was a son who wandered, Hosea 11:1. Here is a Son who grows in wisdom and favor and is obedient, who will keep what the others did not.

The ending of the Bible shows what Simeon saw in advance. In the new creation there is no temple, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, and the nations will walk by its light, Revelation 21:22 to 24. The light for revelation to the Gentiles has become the lamp of the city, and the glory of Israel is the glory of God that lights it. The old man who asked to be dismissed in peace is answered with a world that is at peace for good.

sermon.title: Nunc Dimittis
sermon.why: Begg expounds Luke 2:29-32, Simeon's song at the presentation, showing how this faithful man embraced Jesus as his peace, the glory of Israel, and the light of the world. A faithful, expository handling of the heart of this movement, from a sermon that reads Luke 2:22-32 together.

quiz.q: What did the offering of two birds indicate about Jesus' family?

options.text: They were poor, since two birds were the provision for those who could not afford a lamb.
options.note: Leviticus 12 allowed the poor to bring birds instead of a lamb, marking the family's humble means.

options.text: They were carefully obeying the Law of Moses.
options.note: True, they obeyed the Law, but the specific offering of birds signals their poverty.

options.text: They were wealthy and generous.
options.note: The opposite: the bird offering was the concession for the poor.

options.text: They were disobeying the temple regulations.
options.note: They were fully obedient; the birds were a lawful, prescribed offering.

quiz.q: What did Simeon say when he took the child in his arms?

options.text: His eyes had seen God's salvation, a light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel.
options.note: Verses 30 to 32 are the heart of Simeon's Nunc Dimittis.

options.text: He could now depart in peace as God had promised.
options.note: True and part of the song, but the reason is that he had seen God's salvation, the light for the nations.

options.text: The child would become a great teacher of the Law.
options.note: Simeon proclaimed Him God's salvation and light, far more than a teacher.

options.text: The child would drive the Romans from Israel.
options.note: Simeon spoke of salvation and light for all peoples, not a military deliverance.

quiz.q: What did Simeon foretell to Mary?

options.text: The child would cause the rise and fall of many and be opposed, and a sword would pierce her own soul.
options.note: Verses 34 and 35 give the warning of division and Mary's coming grief.

options.text: The child would be a sign that many would speak against.
options.note: True and stated, but it omits the piercing sword and the rising and falling of many.

options.text: Mary would become a great prophetess like Anna.
options.note: Simeon spoke of the child's mission and Mary's sorrow, not her becoming a prophetess.

options.text: Mary and the child would live a long, untroubled life.
options.note: He foretold opposition and a piercing sword, not an untroubled life.

quiz.q: Why did the boy Jesus stay behind in the temple?

options.text: Because He had to be in His Father's house, as He told His parents.
options.note: Verse 49 gives His own reason, revealing His unique sonship.

options.text: Because He was astounding the teachers with His understanding.
options.note: He did astound them, but His stated reason was that He had to be in His Father's house.

options.text: Because He had become separated from His parents by accident.
options.note: He remained behind purposefully; it was His parents who assumed He was with them.

options.text: Because He was lost and could not find the way home.
options.note: He was not lost; He was deliberately in the temple, His Father's house.

quiz.q: How does Luke describe Jesus' childhood after these events?

options.text: He was obedient to His parents and grew in wisdom and stature and in favor with God and man.
options.note: Verses 51 and 52 summarize His true human growth and obedience.

options.text: He grew strong and was filled with wisdom.
options.note: True and stated in verse 40, but the fuller summary adds His obedience and favor with God and man.

options.text: He immediately began His public ministry.
options.note: He returned to Nazareth and grew for years before His ministry began.

options.text: He stopped submitting to His earthly parents.
options.note: Verse 51 says the opposite: He was obedient to them.

questions: Simeon and Anna waited long years, faithful and prayerful, and were not disappointed. Where are you being called to patient, hopeful waiting on God's promises?
Simeon held the salvation of God in his own arms and could then die in peace. What would it mean for you to find your deepest peace in having seen and received Christ?
Jesus is a light for the Gentiles, salvation prepared in the sight of all peoples. How does the worldwide reach of the gospel shape the way you pray and live?
Simeon warned Mary of a piercing sword. How do you hold together the joy of following Christ with the real cost that discipleship can bring?
At twelve, Jesus was already drawn to His Father's house and His Father's business. Where is God inviting you to make His concerns your own?

translationNotes.note: The Child's father and mother describes Joseph and Mary in their ordinary roles; some later manuscripts read Joseph and His mother, likely to guard the virginal conception, but the meaning is unchanged, since Joseph was His legal father.

In My Father's house is given in a footnote as about My Father's business; the Greek is compact, but either rendering points to Jesus' unique awareness that God is His Father and that He must be occupied with His concerns.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched this session from bible.helloao.org for Luke 2:22-52. Heading, line break, note, and poem markers were skipped when assembling verse text.
